chapter: Movies and the Los Angeles scene
title: Los Angeles clubs without segregation
summary: Asked about L.A.'s segregated scene, Stewart says the Streets of Paris, 331 Club and Swanee Inn were mixed and he saw no problems.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: He was there living. Now, when you came to Los Angeles, what were the circumstances under which musicians worked then, because I know that when in 1945, I think it was, '45 or '46, when Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie came out there, there -- the city, you know, the city was somewhat segregated. The club, I think it played -- I don't know. It was some club that played in Hollywood, had a backwards racial policy, if I remember. And most of the Black bands that came through Los Angeles at that time didn't -- I
think they tended to work on Central Avenue more often.

Central Avenue. Well, I actually didn't run across any situation like that. The couple of places that I worked even with Art Tatum at the Streets of Paris on Hollywood Boulevard, that was -- there was no segregation and like that. Everything was cool, right down to earth.
And, of course, when I worked the 331 Club with Slim and the Swanee Inn with Slim, those, all the clubs that I worked were mixed, and everything was great.
